archetype: WordPress-style ad-supported recipe/food blog (personal narrative + recipe card format)
name: recipe-blog

real_problems.problem: robots.txt contains "Disallow: /recipe-", which by standard prefix matching blocks both actual recipe pages (recipe-chocolate-chip-cookies.html and recipe-banana-bread.html) — the only substantive content on the site.
real_problems.why_it_hurts: Any crawler (search or AI) that respects robots.txt as a simple path-prefix rule will refuse to fetch the two URLs that contain the real recipes, even though a sitemap.xml exists advertising them. The site effectively hides its own core content from well-behaved crawlers while the homepage/about page remain visible, so the brand shows up in the index but its actual product (recipes) does not.

real_problems.problem: sitemap.xml lists only index.html, recipe-chocolate-chip-cookies.html, and about.html; recipe-banana-bread.html is omitted entirely.
real_problems.why_it_hurts: Crawlers or AI ingestion pipelines that seed discovery from the sitemap (rather than purely following in-page links) will never learn that the banana bread page exists, reducing its odds of being indexed or cited even though it is fully linked from the homepage and nav.

real_problems.problem: Neither recipe page includes any schema.org Recipe structured data (JSON-LD) covering ingredients, instructions, yield, or times, despite being unambiguous recipe content.
real_problems.why_it_hurts: AI assistants and search engines that prefer structured data for extracting discrete facts (ingredient lists, cook time, servings) have to fall back to parsing free-form prose mixed with a long narrative, increasing the chance of incomplete or incorrect facts surfacing in citations/answers, and making the page less likely to be selected as an authoritative source for a factual query like "how long do you bake banana bread."

real_problems.problem: Recipe pages have no meta description tag (homepage and about.html both have one).
real_problems.why_it_hurts: When a search engine or AI tool needs a short summary/snippet for these specific pages, it must auto-extract text; given the long personal-story preamble that precedes the recipe in the DOM, the auto-extracted snippet is likely to surface a life-story sentence instead of a recipe summary, weakening how the page is represented in results.

real_problems.where: subscribe-popup.js + email-modal markup on every page
real_problems.problem: A full-screen newsletter modal auto-opens ~1.5s after every page load (home, both recipes, about) and has no persistence mechanism (no cookie/localStorage flag) to suppress it after a visitor has already dismissed it once.
real_problems.why_it_hurts: A visitor closes the popup on the homepage, clicks into a recipe, and the identical popup reopens 1.5 seconds later; it will keep reopening on every subsequent page they visit in the same session. Repeated, unacknowledged interruption of this kind is a well-known driver of visitors abandoning a site rather than reading the content they came for.

real_problems.problem: There is no "Jump to recipe" link/anchor anywhere on either recipe page; roughly 250-350 words of personal narrative sit in the DOM before the recipe card, with no shortcut past them.
real_problems.why_it_hurts: Visitors who land on the page specifically wanting the ingredient list or instructions (the majority of recipe-search traffic) must scroll through unrelated narrative first; the well-documented visitor behavior on this content type is to bounce back to search results rather than scroll, so this measurably reduces on-page engagement and time-on-task completion.

real_problems.problem: An ad block is inserted between almost every individual numbered instruction step inside the recipe card itself, rather than only around the content (header/footer/sidebar).
real_problems.why_it_hurts: It breaks the visual and logical continuity of a short sequential task (cooking steps) into disconnected fragments separated by ad units, forcing a cook to scroll past ads repeatedly while trying to follow along, which is disruptive specifically because this content is meant to be read step-by-step while actively cooking.

real_problems.where: style.css .hero-image rule + usage across all pages
real_problems.problem: Hero images are large (up to 1200x700) but the layout relies on CSS width:100%/height:auto without the images carrying a matching intrinsic aspect ratio reservation beyond their width/height attributes being present only as raw pixel values from a much larger source size, so the rendered box height is only known once each image finishes loading relative to its container width.
real_problems.why_it_hurts: On a content type built around large hero photography, any residual shift as each hero image finishes rendering is proportionally more disruptive to reading flow than on text-heavy pages, nudging the page below and above content around during the first seconds of a visit.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: The long personal-story preamble (grandmother anecdotes, technique backstory) appearing before the recipe card
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: This is a standard, legitimate content-marketing convention for food blogs (adds original long-form text, personal voice, and context that generic recipe aggregators lack). Its mere presence should not be flagged as broken — only the missing in-page shortcut past it (already listed as a real problem) is the actual defect.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: The email-capture modal has a visible, working close (×) button, and clicking the dark backdrop also dismisses it
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: The modal is not a dead-end or focus trap — a visitor can always get rid of it in one click. The genuine defect is narrower and specific: it lacks any memory of that dismissal across page loads, not that it is undismissable.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: Multiple ad slots in the header banner, sidebar widgets, and footer area
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: Ad-supported placement in conventional zones (header, sidebar, between post summaries on the homepage) is the expected, typical monetization model for a recipe blog and is not itself a defect; only the specific mid-instruction-step placement inside the recipe card is flagged.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: Every content image (hero photos and decorative ad placeholders) carries a descriptive, non-generic alt attribute
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: Alt text is present and meaningfully descriptive (e.g. describing the scene, not just the filename) on every hero image, so missing/empty alt text should not be flagged — it was deliberately included correctly precisely because image-heavy pages are often assumed to have this problem.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: Newsletter and comment forms use onsubmit="return false"/preventDefault with no real backend endpoint
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: This is a static test site with no server; a non-functional form submission is expected and appropriate here, not a sign of a broken production feature.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: Every page has a unique, descriptive <title> and a correct self-referencing <link rel="canonical">
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: Titles are not duplicated boilerplate across pages and canonical URLs correctly point to each page's own URL, so this should not be flagged as a duplicate-content or canonicalization problem.

These are legitimate, conventional WordPress-admin-path exclusions and reflect normal, correct robots.txt practice; only the separate /recipe- rule (already flagged) is the actual bug — the overall intent and structure of the robots.txt is sound.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: All internal navigation uses plain relative <a href="..."> links across index.html, both recipe pages, and about.html with no client-side routing/JS gating
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: Every page is reachable via ordinary crawlable anchor tags without requiring JavaScript execution, which is a positive baseline for crawlability and should not be mistaken for a discoverability gap.

notes: Built as a 4-page static WordPress-style food blog (index.html, two recipe posts, about.html) plus robots.txt, sitemap.xml, a shared stylesheet, a shared popup script, and SVG placeholder images for hero photos and ad slots. Two deliberate discoverability landmines were planted for realism: an over-broad robots.txt Disallow rule that accidentally blocks the very pages carrying the recipes, and a sitemap.xml that omits one of the two recipe pages. Engagement problems center on a non-persistent auto-opening newsletter modal, a missing jump-to-recipe shortcut past a deliberately long life-story preamble, and ads spliced between individual numbered cooking steps. Ran the required Semgrep scan on the one newly created script file (subscribe-popup.js); no issues were found, so no fixes were needed.
